notes:
I've read seven sources for these notes:

- Enduring Word (Guzik)
- Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott, both on biblehub
- Matthew Henry, on blueletterbible
- Biblehub's verse pages for 17:3, 17:11 and 17:16, which bring together Gill, Barnes, Benson, Clarke, Poole, Delitzsch and others
- JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown), on studylight
- NET Bible notes on v. 3

**What I couldn't find.** I didn't find any page where a named Protestant tradition argues against another over this chapter. Nothing in my results came from the Catholic, Orthodox or modern-scholarship sites you listed, and nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. I haven't filled those gaps. The only "other view" material below is translation differences in the Catholic Douay-Rheims and Latin Vulgate, which show up on the Bible translation-comparison pages.

---

**v. 1**
- **Breath or spirit?** Ellicott reads "my breath is corrupt," as in the skin disease elephantiasis, and notes that some take it as "my spirit is consumed." He says "graves" means the grave is Job's portion; Hebrew often uses a plural for a singular. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers the physical meaning: foul breath is a sign that death is near. It notes that the verb "extinct" appears nowhere else in Scripture, and reads "graves" as the burial niches cut into a tomb chamber. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Benson takes it as Job's vital strength being used up, his "lamp of life" about to go out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/17-1.htm
- Matthew Henry pictures life as a candle that burns down and can be snuffed out by any accident. The lesson he draws is to use our time well in preparing for eternity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm
- Guzik says Job is carrying on the sense of defeat from chapter 16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the friends started out sympathetic (2:11–13) but became mockers once Job didn't respond the way they expected. That was an especially painful part of his ordeal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Ellicott: Job's eye can see nothing but their provocation, which is a bitter rebuke of his friends. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: they provoked Job and then condemned him for reacting. Treating friends that way in their suffering would test even Job's patience. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm
- JFB: the Hebrew for "continue" literally means "tarry all night," a picture of undisturbed rest. It contrasts with Job's sleepless weeping in 16:20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-17.html

**v. 3** (the key verse, with the widest range of readings)
- **A courtroom request.** The Pulpit Commentary calls these legal terms. Job asks God to come to court with him, to put down the deposit the court would require, and to stand surety for him. "Striking hands" was how a person accepted that responsibility (Prov 6:1). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- **A present token of a future verdict.** Ellicott says Job already has a witness in heaven (16:19) but wants a token now of the vindication to come. He compares Hezekiah's prayer, "undertake for me" (Isa 38:14), and Ps 119:122. He argues that the surety must be divine, God bearing witness to God, and finds this fits remarkably with the later teaching about the persons of the Godhead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- **Christ as the surety (the strongest version).** Gill says the surety Job asks for is Jesus Christ, appointed as Mediator. He says the Old Testament saints knew this, that Job prayed in faith, and that they were pardoned on the strength of Christ's pledge. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/job/17-3.html
- **The gospel in miniature.** Guzik follows the NIV wording: Job is telling God, "You must set this right; I can't." That runs against the friends' view that it was Job's job to repent and fix things. Guzik sees here, in a small way, the New Covenant pattern: God makes the atonement, not us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- **A more careful version.** Matthew Henry says only that "some" see Job glancing at Christ's mediation here: Job knew he couldn't justify himself before God without a mediator. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm
- **A study-note version.** Biblehub's notes link the verse to Heb 7:22, Christ as "the guarantee of a better covenant," and to Rom 8:32, God supplying what he requires. https://biblehub.com/job/17-3.htm
- **A plain courtroom reading, no mediator.** Barnes says the language only seems irreverent because Job is following through the picture of a trial. The idea is: who will guarantee me that God will deal justly? https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/brl/job/17-3.html
- **The Hebrew.** The NET notes say the Hebrew text has two commands in a row ("lay down, pledge me"). Most commentators treat the second as a noun, "lay my pledge beside you." Davidson takes both as verbs for emphasis: "give a pledge, be my surety." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=17&verse=3
- **Catholic translation tradition.** The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin Vulgate, reads very differently: "Deliver me, O Lord, and set me beside thee, and let any man's hand fight against me." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rhe/job/17-3.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God could have opened the friends' minds, so even their lack of sympathy was something he allowed. They are still responsible for it, though, and his withholding understanding is a sign he is displeased with them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Pulpit: God has blinded and hardened them against Job, and he will not exalt people who lack understanding. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: wisdom is God's gift, given at some times and held back at others. People who lack compassion lack understanding to the same degree. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm

**v. 5** (very obscure)
- Ellicott: the Hebrew is literally "for a portion he will tell friends," and its brevity makes it "most obscure." He gives two readings: (a) "denounces friends for a prey," describing how the friends treat Job; (b) a saying about a surety who expects friends to share the cost, but whose children never see them do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- Pulpit: "he that denounceth his friends for a prey" is aimed at the comforters, who hand Job over to disaster by insisting he is secretly guilty. The punishment reaches their children (compare Exod 20:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- JFB: Job is turning back on them their own claims about the wicked man's children (5:4; 15:30). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/job-17.html
- Guzik, keeping the KJV "flattery": Job is defending his own harsh words, since simply flattering his friends would reflect badly on him. He quotes Smick that the verse is a proverb warning about slander. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Older readings of "flattery":
  - The Geneva Bible's note: whoever flatters a man and judges him happy only in prosperity will be punished, along with his descendants.
  - Poole: either they flattered Job with false hopes, or they "flattered" God by judging Job unfairly.
  - Clarke: anyone who relies on friends will be let down, and his children may go hungry waiting.
  - https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/job/17-5.html

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: God made Job a byword for affliction. Yet Job's endurance made him a byword for patience for all time (Jas 5:11). The second line is better translated "an open abhorring" than the KJV's "tabret" (a small drum). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Ellicott gives both options: "tabret," meaning a public warning sign, or "one in whose face they spit." Either way the overall meaning is clear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- Guzik: this is Job's humiliation, which he compares to Christ's descent (Phil 2:5–8). Humiliation is a doorway to grace (Jas 4:6). Job puts the cause in God's sovereignty, not fate, and the friends agreed with him on that much. Guzik also quotes Clarke that "as poor as Job" became a proverb. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: heavy weeping (16:16) dims the eyes, as in Ps 6:7 and 31:9. Being "a shadow" means worn out, unsteady and ready to pass away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: upright people will be shocked that so faithful a man could suffer like this, especially in a world that measured goodness by prosperity. Their shock will turn into indignation at the prosperous wicked. Christians have the key in "perfect through sufferings" (Heb 2:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Ellicott: Job's case will serve as a warning that shocks the upright and encourages the innocent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- Guzik: onlookers could hardly believe a righteous man had been hit so hard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Matthew Henry: Job hopes good people will be surprised by his treatment but won't stumble over it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: "yet" marks a strong contrast. Whatever comes, the righteous keep their course. Job is talking about righteous people in general, who act from principle rather than for reward, and whose goodness gets more settled over time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Guzik calls it a "flash of faith" and sees victory both in enduring and in growing stronger gradually. He quotes F. B. Meyer that believers keep going because Jesus holds them in his hand. He also quotes Clarke, who thought Job was speaking prophetically of his own restoration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Matthew Henry: truly good people keep growing wiser and better, and that progress is a sign their faith is real. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: probably ironic: "come and argue again; I'm confident how it will end." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm
- Pulpit: a challenge to his accusers. Since none of them has shown wisdom (compare 42:8), what they say no longer matters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Guzik: Job insults them as they insulted him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/

**v. 11**
- Several commentators on biblehub's 17:11 page: "thoughts of my heart" is literally "possessions of my heart," the plans Job held dearest.
  - Barnes reflects that death leaves everyone's plans unfinished.
  - Delitzsch connects the verse to the friends' constant calls to repent.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/17-11.htm
- Pulpit: since his life is nearly over, Job no longer cares about clearing his name before people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Guzik: Job now expects a slow decline rather than the quick death he once wanted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Matthew Henry: death ends our plans for this world, but it doesn't end the purpose of a heart that holds fast to the Lord. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: "they" are the friends. They promised that Job's night would turn into day (11:17; also 5:18–26 and 8:21–22), which to him was only more mockery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/17.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Guzik, citing a commentator: in vv. 12–16 Job parodies the friends' advice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/

**vv. 13–14**
- Pulpit: Job expects no recovery, only Sheol as his home. Calling decay "father" means he accepts his lot without complaint. The commentary adds historical background on ancient fears of decay in the grave (embalming, cremation). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Guzik: Job finds a strange comfort in treating the grave as family. Guzik also notes the line could be sarcasm aimed at the friends. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/
- Matthew Henry: when his relatives turned away from him, Job adopted death and the grave as kin instead. We are all "near akin" to decay and worms. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/job/job_017.cfm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: Job doesn't know enough to be dogmatic about Sheol. "Who shall see it?" means: who can see through the dark of the future? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: Job is not without hope. His hope is in things unseen and eternal, not where the friends wanted it, and he points ahead to 19:25. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/17-16.html
- Guzik: Job knows the grave is a thin hope, so the speech ends with hope at war with itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-17/

**v. 16** (grammatically the hardest verse)
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the verb is feminine plural, but "bars" is masculine and "hope" is singular, so the subject is unclear.
  - Ellicott: the verse expresses utter despair.
  - Pulpit: the editor admits he can't attach any satisfactory meaning to the Hebrew. Some read it as "the bars of Sheol shall be broken down," but few commentators accept that.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/17.htm
- Barnes, JFB, Benson and Clarke: Job's hopes go down into the grave with him. Gill adds that they lie locked up there until released by the one who holds the keys of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/17-16.htm
- Delitzsch: Job's real hope is the hope of death, "and consequently the death of hope." When it comes, his suffering will give way to the rest of the grave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/17-16.htm
- Geneva Bible's note: worldly hopes, which the friends took as signs of God's favour, fail, so Job puts his hope in God and in everlasting life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/job/17-16.htm
- Barnes: Job pictured Sheol as gloomy, not a place of punishment but not of joy either. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/17-16.html
- Biblehub's study notes read the verse in light of Job 19:25 and resurrection texts (Ps 16:10; Isa 26:19). https://biblehub.com/job/17-16.htm
- The NASB footnote gives another possible Hebrew reading: "Let my limbs sink down to Sheol." https://www.blueletterbible.org/verse/nasb20/job/17/16/
- The Douay-Rheims has "All that I have shall go down into the deepest pit," and asks whether Job will at least find rest there. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/job/17-16.html

---

**Where readers really differ (not divided by tradition in what I found):**
- **v. 3:**
  - Gill reads it as Christ the surety, and Guzik as a picture of the gospel.
  - Ellicott and Pulpit see the Trinity "fitting" the language, while reading the verse itself as a legal plea.
  - Henry mentions the Christ reading only cautiously, and Barnes reads it as courtroom language alone.
- **vv. 15–16:** Henry and the Geneva note find a hope beyond death here. Delitzsch, Ellicott and Barnes see despair.
